manifest.hint: A go.mod names the module, and only you can choose that name. Run `go mod init <module path>` here, then re-run jig.

toolchain.why: Runs the whole third-party analyzer set (errcheck, staticcheck, gosec, revive, testifylint, forbidigo...) in one pass over the type-checked package graph, which is the only place rule ids like SA1019 or G402 are reachable from a single command.
toolchain.configSample:
version: "2"
run:
  timeout: 5m
  tests: true
linters:
  default: none
  enable:
    - bodyclose
    - contextcheck
    - depguard
    - errcheck
    - errorlint
    - forbidigo
    - gochecknoglobals
    - gocritic
    - gosec
    - govet
    - ineffassign
    - nilerr
    - noctx
    - nolintlint
    - revive
    - staticcheck
    - testifylint
    - thelper
    - unparam
    - unused
    - usetesting
  settings:
    errcheck:
      check-type-assertions: true
      check-blank: true
    forbidigo:
      analyze-types: true
      forbid:
        - p: ^fmt\.Print.*$
          msg: debug print left in committed code
        - p: ^testing\.T\.Skip.*$
          msg: a skipped test is an unrun test
        - p: ^os\.Exit$
          msg: return an error instead of exiting
        - p: ^log\.Fatal.*$
          msg: return an error instead of exiting
    govet:
      enable:
        - appends
        - assign
        - atomic
        - bools
        - buildtag
        - copylocks
        - defers
        - directive
        - errorsas
        - httpresponse
        - ifaceassert
        - loopclosure
        - lostcancel
        - nilfunc
        - printf
        - shift
        - stdmethods
        - stringintconv
        - structtag
        - tests
        - unmarshal
        - unreachable
        - unusedresult
        - waitgroup
    nolintlint:
      require-explanation: true
      require-specific: true
      allow-unused: false
    revive:
      rules:
        - name: unhandled-error
        - name: empty-block
        - name: deep-exit
        - name: bare-return
        - name: context-as-argument
    testifylint:
      enable:
        - bool-compare
        - compares
        - empty
        - error-is-as
        - error-nil
        - expected-actual
        - float-compare
        - go-require
        - len
        - nil-compare
        - require-error
        - suite-dont-use-pkg
        - useless-assert
    depguard:
      rules:
        main:
          list-mode: lax
          deny:
            - pkg: math/rand$
              desc: use math/rand/v2 or crypto/rand
formatters:
  enable:
    - gofumpt
  settings:
    gofumpt:
      extra-rules: true

verify.expected: exit code 1 and a line of the form path/to/file.go:12:2: Error return value of `f.Close` is not checked (errcheck)

toolchain.why: A stricter superset of gofmt; it is the only step that normalises the diff shape, so a session cannot smuggle a reformat-the-world change past review as part of a one-line fix.

verify.expected: prints the path of every unformatted file; empty output means clean

toolchain.why: Go has no separate type checker - vet runs go/types over every package and then the standard analyzer set (printf, tests, copylocks, lostcancel, httpresponse, loopclosure), catching type-level and semantic mistakes the compiler accepts.

go 1.25.0

verify.expected: exit code 1 and a line of the form ./x_test.go:9:6: TestFoo has malformed name: first letter after 'Test' must not be lowercase

toolchain.why: The only step that proves behaviour; -race, -count=1 and -shuffle=on together defeat the three ways a green run can lie (data races, cached results, order dependence).
toolchain.configSample:

go 1.25.0

	github.com/stretchr/testify v1.11.1
)

verify.expected: exit code 1 with FAIL lines; a seeded skip shows as --- SKIP with ok ... [no tests to run] rather than a pass

toolchain.why: Compiles every package including ones no test imports, so an invented identifier, a wrong signature or an import path that does not resolve fails here even when the test binary never touches it.
toolchain.wiring: Makefile target: build: ; go build ./... && go mod tidy -diff

toolchain.why: Cross-references the module graph against the Go vulnerability database and reports only the advisories whose vulnerable symbols are actually reachable from this code - dependency risk that no lint rule sees.
toolchain.configSample:
module example.com/project

go 1.25.0

verify.expected: non-zero exit and 'Your code is affected by N vulnerabilities' with a GO-YYYY-NNNN id and a call stack; 'No vulnerabilities found.' when clean

classes.title: Test skipped instead of fixed
agentModes: adds t.Skip with a 'flaky, revisit' message when it cannot make the assertion pass
skips the one failing case in a table so the package reports ok
converts a red test to a skip and reports the suite as green

forbid.msg: a skipped test is an unrun test

classes.gapNotes: Cannot tell a legitimate environment guard (if testing.Short() { t.Skip() } or a skip behind a build-gated integration flag) from an abandoned test - both trip. It also misses the opposite move: deleting the test function outright, which leaves no token to match.

evidence.source: testing.T.Skip / Skipped in the Go testing package docs; forbidigo pattern syntax and analyze-types from its README, which documents <package>.<type>.<method> matching, wired through golangci-lint linters.settings.forbidigo

classes.title: Test body removed but the function kept
agentModes: empties a failing test's body so the name still appears in the run and the package passes
replaces the assertions with an early return after failing to diagnose the fault
keeps the function as a placeholder it intends to refill and never does
classes.gapNotes: Only the fully empty and bare-return shapes match. A body reduced to `_ = subject` or a single `t.Log` still looks populated, and a test deleted from the file leaves nothing to match at all - that needs a diff against the previous commit or a coverage floor.

evidence.source: Go test function signature convention from the testing package docs; no linter in the golangci-lint set reports an empty test body, so this is regex-only by design

classes.title: Failing assertion softened into a log line
agentModes: swaps t.Fatalf for t.Logf so a mismatch is recorded but the test still passes
keeps the comparison and drops the failure call after it cannot reproduce the expected value
reports the suite as green because every case now only logs
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic: it only recognises the guard-then-log shape with a handful of conventional variable names. The commoner softening - widening the expected value, asserting on len() instead of contents, or replacing require.Equal with assert.NotNil - changes no token this pattern watches. testifylint's require-error only applies to projects that use testify.

evidence.source: testifylint checker ids require-error and useless-assert are both enabled-by-default checkers in its README table; the regex shape is reasoned from Go's standard table-test idiom

classes.title: Error discarded into the blank identifier
agentModes: writes _ = f.Close() to make errcheck or the compiler stop complaining
silences an error it could not diagnose rather than wrapping and returning it
uses _, _ = w.Write(b) to get past an unused-variable error
classes.gapNotes: The regex matches any blank assignment from any call and has no idea whether the discarded value is an error at all, so `_ = buf.Len()` and `_, _ = fmt.Fprintln(w, s)` read exactly like a swallowed Close error. Only errcheck, which is type-aware, knows the difference. It also cannot see the more common shape - calling an error-returning function and assigning nothing at all - because the regex has no way to know the callee's arity.

evidence.source: errcheck's check-blank option is documented in golangci-lint's linters settings page: 'Report about assignment of errors to blank identifier'

classes.title: Error-returning call left unchecked
agentModes: calls an error-returning function as a statement because the happy path is all it modelled
drops the error branch when rewriting a function to fit a new signature
leaves defer f.Close() with no error handling in a write path, losing data on a full disk
classes.gapNotes: Tool-rule only on purpose: whether a bare call statement discards an error depends on the callee's signature, which regex cannot resolve. errcheck also ships default exclusions (fmt.Print family, bytes.Buffer writes), so a genuinely dropped error inside an excluded function stays invisible unless disable-default-exclusions is set.

evidence.source: errcheck and revive are both in the golangci-lint linter list; revive's rule id unhandled-error appears verbatim in revive's RULES_DESCRIPTIONS.md

classes.title: Panic swallowed by a bare recover
agentModes: wraps a crashing handler in defer func(){ recover() }() to make the test stop panicking
adds a recover it never inspects after failing to find the nil dereference
keeps the process alive by discarding the panic value, so the fault never reaches a log
classes.gapNotes: Matches only the immediate defer-closure form. A recover captured into a variable that is then ignored (r := recover(); _ = r), or a recover hidden in a named helper called from defer, both pass. No linter in the golangci-lint set has a confirmed rule for a discarded recover value, so there is no tool-rule backstop here.

evidence.source: recover semantics from the Go language spec; no rule id claimed because none was confirmed in the golangci-lint linter list

classes.title: Nil returned from the error branch
agentModes: returns nil inside if err != nil to satisfy a single-value signature it did not want to change
keeps the check for appearances while dropping the failure, so callers see a zero value as success
narrows a two-value return to one value and loses the error on the way
classes.gapNotes: Only the single-value `return nil` shape matches. The multi-value equivalent (return result, nil after a failed step) and returning a zero struct instead of nil both slip past the regex; nilerr covers the multi-value case but only when the error variable is in scope and unmistakably non-nil.

evidence.source: nilerr is listed in the golangci-lint linter list (finds code returning nil even though it checks that the error is not nil)

classes.title: Library code kills the process
agentModes: reaches for log.Fatalf inside a package because it is the shortest way to stop on an error
adds os.Exit to a helper so a failing path stops without touching the signature
turns a recoverable error into a panic to make the caller compile
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic because package main is where os.Exit belongs: the pattern has no path exclusion for main.go or cmd/, so every CLI entry point trips it and has to be waved off once. It also does not catch bare panic() - too many legitimate uses in Go to flag flatly - nor a logger value whose Fatal method is called through a variable (logger.Fatal), which the package-qualified pattern cannot see.

evidence.source: revive rule id deep-exit appears in RULES_DESCRIPTIONS.md; forbidigo's simple-regex pattern form (^fmt\.Print.*$) is the documented syntax in golangci-lint's linters settings page

classes.title: Type assertion taken without the ok result
agentModes: asserts any to a concrete type in one value because the two-value form did not fit the expression it was writing
converts a type switch into a direct assertion while simplifying a function
asserts an interface it inferred rather than read, turning a wrong guess into a runtime panic

fixtures.violation:
package eventbus

func (b *Bus) dispatch(e any) {
	msg := e.(*OrderPlaced)
	b.orders <- msg

	meta := e.(Metadata)
	b.audit(meta.TraceID)
}

classes.gapNotes: Only the assign-to-one-name shape is matched; an assertion used inline as an argument (handle(e.(*OrderPlaced))) or in a return statement is not on a line the pattern recognises. errcheck with check-type-assertions covers those, but only when the linter can type-check the package.

evidence.source: errcheck's check-type-assertions option in golangci-lint's linters settings page: 'Report about not checking of errors in type assertions: a := b.(MyStruct)'

classes.title: Type widened to any to silence the compiler
agentModes: changes a parameter or field to any after the compiler rejects the value it wanted to pass
returns map[string]any instead of modelling the struct it could not find
replaces a named type with interface{} rather than fix the mismatch the error pointed at
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic and blunt: `any` is legitimate in decoders, log attribute lists and anything mirroring encoding/json, and every one of those trips. The near-miss shows the trap it does avoid - `any` as a generic type constraint in [T any] is not a widened parameter. Nothing here sees the widening that matters most, an exported field changed from a concrete type to any between commits; that needs a diff, not a snapshot. No golangci-lint rule was found that distinguishes justified from lazy `any`, so there is no tool-rule.

evidence.source: Go 1.18 type-parameter and `any` alias syntax from the language spec; no rule id claimed because none was confirmed

classes.title: Blanket nolint directive with no linter and no reason
agentModes: adds //nolint above the line the linter flagged instead of fixing what it flagged
writes //nolint:all to clear a whole file of findings at once
suppresses a gosec or errcheck report it did not understand and moves on
classes.gapNotes: The pattern reads only the two blanket forms, a bare //nolint and //nolint:all. A specific directive left unexplained (//nolint:errcheck on its own) is nolintlint's require-explanation to catch, and one carrying a fake reason (//nolint:errcheck // safe) satisfies both halves, because nolintlint judges the form of the explanation and never whether it is true. Suppression moved into .golangci.yml as a linters.exclusions rule is invisible to this class entirely, and a project without golangci-lint keeps only the pattern.

evidence.source: nolintlint is in the golangci-lint linter list ('reports ill-formed or insufficient nolint directives') with settings require-explanation, require-specific and allow-unused

classes.title: Debug print left in committed code
agentModes: instruments a function with fmt.Println while chasing a bug and never removes the calls
prints intermediate state instead of adding an assertion or a structured log line
leaves prints in a hot path where they become an unformatted, unlevelled log

forbid.msg: debug print left in committed code

classes.gapNotes: A CLI whose actual output is fmt.Println will trip on every legitimate line, so this class needs a path exclusion for cmd/ that the pattern list does not express. It also misses prints routed through a named writer (fmt.Fprintln(os.Stdout, ...)), which is the same mistake wearing a different call.

evidence.source: forbidigo's documented example patterns ^fmt\.Print.*$ and ^print(ln)?$ appear verbatim in golangci-lint's linters settings page

classes.title: Credential hardcoded in source
agentModes: inlines a key or password it saw in a log, a fixture or the conversation to make a call succeed
invents a plausible-looking token so the code compiles and the test reaches the network stub
replaces a failing os.Getenv lookup with the literal value rather than wire up the variable
classes.gapNotes: The pattern requires the value to contain a digit and to not look like an ALL_CAPS env-var name, which is what keeps the near-miss clean - but it also means a lowercase alphabetic secret ('correcthorsebattery') is missed, and a credential stored in a variable whose name avoids the listed words is missed entirely. gosec G101 is entropy- and name-based and carries its own false-positive rate, hence heuristic on both detectors. Neither sees a secret committed to a .env, a testdata fixture or a YAML manifest, since paths here are Go source only.

evidence.source: gosec rule G101 'Look for hardcoded credentials' from gosec's RULES.md; runnable through golangci-lint's gosec linter

classes.title: TLS certificate verification turned off
agentModes: sets InsecureSkipVerify: true to get past an x509 error it could not diagnose
copies a snippet that disables verification to make a local call to a self-signed endpoint work
leaves the flag on after the debugging session that motivated it
classes.gapNotes: Only the literal true is matched: InsecureSkipVerify: cfg.AllowInsecure passes the regex, and gosec's G402 also reasons about literals, so a config-driven bypass that defaults to true in production is caught by neither. Verification disabled by supplying a permissive VerifyPeerCertificate or a custom RootCAs pool containing an attacker CA is out of reach of both.

evidence.source: gosec rule G402 'Look for bad TLS connection settings' from gosec's RULES.md; crypto/tls field name from the standard library

classes.title: Broken hash or non-cryptographic randomness in a security path
agentModes: reaches for md5 or sha1 because they are the examples it has seen most
uses math/rand to generate a token or nonce, which is deterministic given the seed
keeps a weak primitive after being told the output only needs to look unique
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic because md5 over a cache key and math/rand for jitter or test data are both legitimate, and the regex cannot see the use site's intent. It also cannot tell math/rand's rand.Intn from math/rand/v2's, and it misses a weak primitive reached through an interface or a hash.Hash variable. gosec G401/G404 have the same blind spot but add the import-blocklist angle via G501.

evidence.source: gosec RULES.md: G401 'Detect the usage of MD5 or SHA1', G404 'Insecure random number source (rand)', G501 'Import blocklist: crypto/md5'

classes.title: SQL assembled with Sprintf or concatenation
agentModes: builds the query with fmt.Sprintf because the placeholder dialect it guessed was rejected
concatenates a filter clause from a request field to make a dynamic search work
switches from parameters to interpolation when the driver returned a bind error it could not read
classes.gapNotes: Only catches interpolation written at the call site. A query built into a variable on an earlier line and then passed by name (q := "..." + filter; db.Query(q)) defeats the regex completely - that is exactly what gosec G201/G202 are there for, and they too need the taint to stay inside one function. The method list is database/sql's own, so a query interpolated into a call on sqlx, GORM or a generated repository wrapper is not on a line this pattern recognises.

evidence.source: gosec RULES.md: G201 'SQL query construction using format string', G202 'SQL query construction using string concatenation'; database/sql method names from the standard library

classes.title: HTTP response body left unclosed
agentModes: writes http.Get and decodes the body without a defer, leaking a connection per call
drops the defer when refactoring a request helper into a shorter form
uses the context-free convenience functions so a cancelled request keeps running
classes.gapNotes: Tool-rule only: closing is proved by the absence of a defer, and no regex can assert an absence across a function body without producing noise on every correct call site. bodyclose works on the SSA of one function, so a response returned to a caller that closes it is reported as a leak, and a body closed inside a helper is missed. The missing-context half of the third agent mode is uncovered here: noctx reports calls made without a context.Context and never looks at whether a body is closed, so it is not a detector for this class. go vet's httpresponse only catches the defer-before-error-check ordering mistake, not an absent close.

evidence.source: bodyclose is in the golangci-lint linter list; httpresponse is in the default go vet analyzer set listed under cmd/vet ('check for mistakes using HTTP responses')

classes.title: context.TODO left where a real context belongs
agentModes: passes context.TODO() rather than thread a ctx parameter through the call chain it would have to change
keeps the placeholder from a scaffold it generated and never revisits it
breaks cancellation and deadline propagation without any compile-time signal
classes.gapNotes: Deliberately does not flag context.Background(), because that is correct in main, in package-level initialisation and in tests - which means the commonest form of the same mistake, calling context.Background() inside a function that already has a ctx parameter, is left to contextcheck. contextcheck is heuristic and does not run reliably across package boundaries.

evidence.source: contextcheck is in the golangci-lint linter list ('check whether the function uses a non-inherited context'); context.TODO semantics from the standard library docs

classes.title: Test mutates process globals instead of using the testing helpers
agentModes: calls os.Setenv in a test with no cleanup, so the next test in the binary sees the leaked variable
creates a temp dir with os.MkdirTemp and never removes it
chdirs the process to fix a relative path, which breaks every test scheduled after it under -shuffle=on
classes.gapNotes: Only the four os calls listed are seen. A test that mutates a package-level variable, registers a global http.DefaultServeMux handler, or writes into a shared testdata directory leaks exactly as badly and matches nothing. t.Setenv is itself incompatible with t.Parallel, which neither detector checks. os.MkdirTemp is in the pattern for consistency with usetesting's os-mkdir-temp, but it mutates nothing global - it leaks an uncleaned directory - so that alternative reports a different defect than the class title names.

evidence.source: usetesting is in the golangci-lint linter list; its os-setenv, os-mkdir-temp, os-chdir and os-temp-dir options are documented in its readme, with os-chdir requiring Go >= 1.24 for t.Chdir

classes.title: Test command narrowed or its failure suppressed
agentModes: appends || true to the test step so a red suite still reports a green job
narrows the run to -run TestSmoke and calls the suite passing
drops -race or adds -short so the case that was failing no longer executes

fixtures.violation:
name: ci
on: [push]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v6
        with:
          go-version: '1.25'
      - name: unit tests
        run: go test -short -run TestSmoke ./... || true
fixtures.nearMiss:
name: ci
on: [push]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v6
        with:
          go-version: '1.25'
      - name: unit tests
        run: go test -race -shuffle=on -count=1 -coverprofile=coverage.out ./...
      - name: vet
        run: go vet ./...

classes.gapNotes: Sees only what is committed. A session that runs a narrowed command in its own shell and then claims the suite passed leaves no trace in any file, and a package silently dropped from the ./... expansion by an unsatisfiable build tag is invisible here too. Nothing checks that -race is present - only that the listed weakenings are absent. The command has to be spelled go test literally, so a Makefile recipe that runs $(GOTEST) or a script that calls a wrapper function hides every flag behind a name the pattern never reads, and a quoted narrowing (-run 'TestSmoke') does not match the flag alternatives either.

evidence.source: go test flag semantics from cmd/go: -count=1 is 'the idiomatic way to disable test caching', -shuffle=on seeds order from the system clock (Go 1.17+), -race enables the data race detector

classes.title: Filesystem replace directive left in go.mod
agentModes: adds replace => ../lib to make a local edit visible and never removes it, so the build works only on that machine
points a module at a scratch checkout to get past a version it could not resolve
leaves the directive in the commit, breaking every clone and every CI runner

fixtures.violation:
module example.com/service

go 1.25.0

require (
	example.com/lib v1.4.0
	github.com/google/go-cmp v0.7.0
)

replace example.com/lib => ../lib
fixtures.nearMiss:
module example.com/service

go 1.25.0

require (
	example.com/lib v1.4.0
	github.com/google/go-cmp v0.7.0
)

// replace example.com/lib => ../lib // local debugging only, never commit uncommented
replace example.com/lib => example.com/lib v1.4.1-rc.2

classes.gapNotes: Only the block-free single-line form anchored at column zero is matched; a replace inside a parenthesised replace ( ... ) block is indented and slips through. It also says nothing about the neighbouring abuses - a downgraded `go` directive, an exclude, or a go.work file that redirects modules outside the repository.

evidence.source: go.mod replace directive syntax from the Go modules reference (cmd/go); a replacement path beginning with ./ or ../ is a filesystem path by definition

classes.title: Import path that the module does not declare or that does not exist
agentModes: imports a package it inferred from the API it wished existed, with a plausible module path and version suffix
adds a third-party dependency for something the standard library already covers
leaves go.mod out of sync with the imports it wrote, so the build works only where the module cache is warm
classes.gapNotes: Tool-rule only: no regex can tell an invented module path from a real one, and depguard in strict mode only proves the import is outside the declared allowlist - a typo inside an allowed prefix, or an invented function on a package that does exist, still needs `go build ./...` and `go mod tidy -diff`, which are wired as toolchain steps rather than detectors because neither has rule ids. The allowlist in the options is per-project and must be filled with the real module path and dependencies.

evidence.source: depguard is in the golangci-lint linter list; its rules/list-mode/allow/deny keys with the $gostd shorthand appear verbatim in golangci-lint's linters settings page

classes.title: Deprecated standard library or dependency API used
agentModes: writes ioutil.ReadFile and other pre-1.16 forms because they dominate its training material
reaches for a deprecated option struct field the docs marked years ago
reintroduces a deprecated call while rewriting a function that had already been migrated
classes.gapNotes: Tool-rule only: deprecation lives in a // Deprecated: doc comment on the declaration, which only a type-aware analyzer can follow to the call site - a name list in a regex would rot immediately. SA1019 sees nothing when the dependency marks a symbol deprecated in prose without the conventional comment prefix.

evidence.source: staticcheck check SA1019 'Using a deprecated function, variable, constant or field' from staticcheck.dev/docs/checks; io/ioutil deprecation from the Go 1.16 release notes
